I found good material from the older commentaries and evangelical sources. I found nothing on the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran or Pentecostal-specific sites, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching about this chapter. Some tool calls failed, so several notes rely on search-result excerpts rather than full pages.

---

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- **"The word that came to Jeremiah" is a heading, not the start of a prophecy.** Ellicott points out that no actual prophecy follows until 42:7. He reads the line as a heading for the prophecies given after the city fell. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-1.htm
- **Where the "word" actually is: the commentators split.**
  - Benson, Matthew Henry, and the Jewish commentators Rashi ("Jarchi") and Kimchi (as reported by Gill) point to 42:7. Gill thinks a more general title, as Abarbanel holds, fits best. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-1.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/40-1.html
  - Keil & Delitzsch read it as the heading for chapters 40–45 as a whole, like the heading in 1:1–3. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-1.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary rejects that view. It suggests the original prophecy under this heading was lost or moved elsewhere. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-1.htm
  - The Restoration Commentary takes "the word" broadly, covering history as well as prophecy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-40.html
- **Ramah.** Ellicott places it in Benjamin, about six miles from Jerusalem. It served as a holding camp where prisoners waited for Nebuzaradan to decide their fate. He thinks the captain and the prophet had not met before. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-1.htm
- **Why Jeremiah was in chains.** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown gives two options: carelessness by his guards, or (following Calvin) Nebuzaradan wanting to shame the people for jailing the prophet. Guzik, quoting Harrison, says Jeremiah was chained even though Nebuchadnezzar had ordered him treated well. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-1.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-40/
- **Fitting this with 39:14.** The Pulpit Commentary sees an apparent conflict with 39:14. It explains this by the shortness of the earlier account and prefers the fuller version here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-1.htm

**vv. 2–3**
- **A pagan states God's judgment.** Guzik says Nebuzaradan knew Jeremiah's prophecies and believed God's word more than God's own covenant people did. Quoting Feinberg, he suggests Nebuzaradan was repeating the main point of Jeremiah's preaching. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-40/
- **Ellicott:** it is significant that the Babylonian general speaks as if he recognised Jehovah as Israel's God and Jeremiah as His messenger. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-1.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** the captain seems to boast that he was God's tool to fulfil what Jeremiah foretold. Many people can see God's justice toward others but are blind to their own sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-1.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):**
  - The people deserved a preacher like Nebuzaradan, because they had been deaf to God's patient warnings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-40.html
  - The "you" seems to include Jeremiah, but Calvin argues Nebuzaradan was actually praising Jeremiah's faithfulness, not counting him among the sinners. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-40.html
- **Pett:** Nebuzaradan probably knew Jeremiah's message from Babylonian spies. For the reader, the key point is that Babylon's own official admits the LORD had not failed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/jeremiah-40.html
- **Chuck Smith:** God always keeps His word. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/jeremiah-40.html
- **Critical view:** the Restoration Commentary reports that "most commentators" treat vv. 2–3 as a later addition, since a pagan supposedly could not talk like this. It disagrees: Nebuzaradan may simply have heard Jeremiah's predictions and been struck by how they came true. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-40.html

**v. 4**
- **Why Nebuzaradan freed him.** Guzik thinks it was respect for Jeremiah's courage, together with his message of surrender, which suited Babylon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-40/
- **A rare choice.** Guzik notes the other exiles were forced to go, while Jeremiah was one of the few allowed to choose. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-40/
- **Calvin:** while the whole nation went into bondage, Jeremiah alone was free to go wherever he wished. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-40.html
- **Matthew Henry:**
  - "I will look well to you" literally means "I will set my eye upon you." It promises respect and protection, not just basic care. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/40-1.html
  - Jeremiah could even go to Anathoth and enjoy the field he had bought. The man recently moved from prison to prison could now walk freely. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_040.cfm
- **Bible Hub study notes:**
  - The choice shows both God's providence and human free will. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/jeremiah/40.htm
  - It also pictures the believer's daily choice between comfort and calling. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/jeremiah/40.htm

**v. 5**
- **"Before Jeremiah turned to go."** The Hebrew is hard here.
  - Keil & Delitzsch read it as the narrator's aside: Jeremiah still hadn't decided, so Nebuzaradan settled it for him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-6.htm
  - Barnes reports that most modern commentators render it "as he still gave no answer." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-6.htm
  - Matthew Henry sees the same hesitation, which Nebuzaradan resolves; he adds that "sudden thoughts sometimes prove wise ones." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_040.cfm
- **Gedaliah.**
  - Guzik, quoting Feinberg, says Nebuchadnezzar had lost all faith in David's line, so he chose an experienced official who was not royal. He also mentions a seal from Lachish naming a "Gedaliah" who was palace governor, possibly the same man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-40/
  - Pett says the title "governor over the cities of Judah" shows Jerusalem no longer mattered politically. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/jeremiah-40.html
- **Calvin:**
  - Nebuzaradan sent Jeremiah to Gedaliah to keep him safe in a land that was still "like a den of robbers." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-40.html
  - The two gifts were food and a present. God arranged for a pagan to treat Jeremiah more kindly than the "children of Abraham" had. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-40.html
- **God's provision.** Guzik, quoting F. B. Meyer, says God can feed His servants through ravens, a widow, or a Babylonian captain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-40/
- **Matthew Henry:** without these supplies Jeremiah might have died in the ruined land. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_040.cfm

**v. 6**
- **Most commentators praise Jeremiah's choice.**
  - Guzik says he stayed because he loved his people. He quotes Morgan on Jeremiah turning down safety in Babylon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-40/
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Gill compare the choice to Moses choosing to suffer with God's people (Hebrews 11:24–26). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-6.htm
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown adds that it proves his motives were pure when he earlier tried to leave the city (37:12–14). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-6.htm
- **The one dissenting voice.** Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary says it is "doubtful whether Jeremiah acted right." It adds that people who long for others' good tend to hope for better times from small signs. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-6.htm
- **Calvin:** staying showed Jeremiah's firmness, though turning down Nebuzaradan's kind offer risked giving offence. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/40-6.html
- **Mizpah.**
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the Mizpah in Benjamin, not the one in Gilead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-6.htm
  - Constable: it became the centre of Babylon's government in Judah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-40.html
- **Pett:** Jeremiah felt a pastoral duty to the people left behind. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/jeremiah-40.html

**vv. 7–8**
- **The army commanders.** Guzik says these officers had to choose between underground resistance and accepting Babylonian rule. They came to find out whether Gedaliah would rebel, as Zedekiah had. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-40/
- **Ishmael.**
  - Pett says he is named first because he was of royal blood, and he would soon prove a traitor. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/jeremiah-40.html
  - Clarke says he may have sheltered with Baalis during the siege. https://studylight.org/commentaries/acc/jeremiah-40.html
- **The other names.** The Restoration Commentary places Netophah near Bethlehem and notes that Johanan later led the remnant to Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-40.html
- **Who was left.** Guzik, quoting Thompson, says most were poor, but some royal princesses and army remnants remained too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-40/
- **Calvin:** making Gedaliah governor was God honouring the man who had once saved Jeremiah's life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-40.html

**v. 9**
- **Guzik:** Gedaliah's oath assured the officers that the wisest course was to accept God's judgment through Babylon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-40/
- **Matthew Henry:** "Fear not to serve" means "fear not the sin of it." In other words, submitting is not wrong. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_040.cfm
- **The Restoration Commentary:**
  - Gedaliah promised no reprisals. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-40.html
  - He may have won the fighters an amnesty from Nebuchadnezzar. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-40.html
- **Pett:** Gedaliah had probably been briefed by Nebuchadnezzar on what terms to offer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/jeremiah-40.html
- **Bible Hub study notes:** these notes connect Gedaliah's advice with Jeremiah's letter to the exiles (29:4–7) and with Romans 13:1–4. They add the condition "when it aligns with God's purposes." https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/jeremiah/40.htm

**v. 10**
- **"To represent you" (literally "to stand before").** Barnes says Gedaliah would be Babylon's minister. Visiting officials would act through him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/40-10.html
- **Guzik:** Gedaliah was repeating Jeremiah's own counsel: accept the judgment and honour God in ordinary life. Quoting Harrison, he adds that Gedaliah's job included collecting tribute from the harvest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-40/
- **"The cities you have taken."**
  - Calvin thinks they hadn't captured towns by force. It simply meant "stay wherever you are." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-40.html
  - Barnes says each captain had probably seized a base, and Gedaliah let them keep it to build trust. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/40-10.html
- **Season.** Gill says these were tree fruits, because the grain harvests were already over. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/40-10.html
- **Why Mizpah.** The Restoration Commentary says archaeologists have found no sign that it was destroyed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-40.html

**vv. 11–12**
- **Guzik:** once the land settled, refugees came home and enjoyed a measure of blessing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-40/
- **Matthew Henry:**
  - Gedaliah let the people enjoy the harvest and, as far as we know, demanded no tribute. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_040.cfm
  - Even so, Jeremiah had never promised good days straight after the fall; it was Providence that seemed to raise such hopes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-14.htm
- **Trapp:** God often rewards those who love their country. **Kretzmann:** the harvest was bigger because so few people were left. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/40-12.html
- **Bible Hub study notes:** these notes see a taste of the "good figs" blessing (Jer. 24) here. They also find echoes of the jubilee year in Leviticus 25. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/jeremiah/40.htm

**vv. 13–14**
- **Baalis.**
  - Ellicott: he was probably allied with Zedekiah (27:3). He and the royal Ishmael fell back on assassination once open revolt was impossible. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-14.htm
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the name comes from Baal, and Ishmael later fled to Ammon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-14.htm
- **Motives.**
  - The Cambridge Bible says Ishmael's motive is easy to see: wounded royal pride. Baalis's motive is less clear. It might be a grudge against Jeremiah's friends, or a plan to grab territory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-14.htm
  - Keil & Delitzsch say Baalis's motive cannot be known. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-14.htm
  - Constable adds that unrest in Judah would keep Nebuchadnezzar's attention away from Ammon. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-40.html
- **"Take your life."** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Gill give the literal sense as "strike you in the soul," meaning a fatal blow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-14.htm
- **Why Gedaliah didn't believe it.** Gill thinks Ishmael had probably acted friendly and courteous. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/ubv/jeremiah/40-14.html

**v. 15**
- **Poole:** Johanan went to Gedaliah privately because the public warning was being ignored. He argued that the whole remnant depended on Gedaliah's life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-15.htm
- **Constable:** Johanan offered to kill Ishmael secretly to protect both Gedaliah and the community. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-40.html
- **Bible Hub study notes:** these notes compare the moment to David sparing Saul (1 Samuel 24), where convenience is weighed against moral restraint. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/jeremiah/40.htm

**v. 16**
- **Most commentators call Gedaliah noble but naive.**
  - Clarke: "noble Gedaliah lost his life by not believing that evil of others of which he himself was incapable." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/40-16.html
  - Matthew Henry: he had "more of the innocency of the dove than the wisdom of the serpent." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_040.cfm
  - Ellicott: he would not approve one crime to prevent another. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/40-14.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed) gives the most balanced view.** Rushing to condemn Ishmael would have been wrong, because believing every accusation leaves no one innocent. Still, Gedaliah could have protected himself, and he wronged Johanan by calling him a liar. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/40-16.html
- **He should have asked God.** Constable says Gedaliah would have been wise to seek the Lord's will through Jeremiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/40-16.html Kidner (quoted by Guzik) says the same, but adds that this is "easily said." https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/jeremiah/jeremiah-40.cfm
- **The Restoration Commentary:** it is hard to tell whether Gedaliah was being naive or brave. He may have dismissed the threat to keep the leaders' confidence. He was right to forbid the killing, but he should have guarded himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-40.html
- **Chuck Smith:** the lesson is to listen to God's warnings. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/40-12.html

---

## Where Protestant traditions differ
I found no real split between denominations on this chapter. The disagreements cut across traditions and are about how to read the text:
- what the heading in v. 1 refers to;
- whether Jeremiah was wise to stay (v. 6), where Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary stands nearly alone;
- whether Gedaliah's trust was a virtue or a failing (v. 16).

Calvin's view on v. 16 is the most developed Reformed position. I found no Wesleyan, Lutheran or Pentecostal comment on these verses.

## Other views
- **Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey):** Gedaliah came from a leading Jerusalem family; his father and grandfather served at Josiah's court. People at the time suspected him of collaborating with Babylon, yet he restored order with help from the officers and Jeremiah. https://studylight.bibleodyssey.org/dictionary/gedaliah/ Mizpah became Babylon's provincial capital. Bible Odyssey's Mizpah entry calls Gedaliah's killers "nationalistic zealots." https://thesacredpage.bibleodyssey.org/dictionary/mizpah/
- **Critical theories:** the possibly lost prophecy (v. 1) and vv. 2–3 as a later addition, both covered above.
- **Jewish tradition:** later Jews kept a yearly Fast of Gedaliah to mourn his murder. https://biblehub.com/q/who_was_gedaliah_in_the_bible.htm
- **Catholic, Orthodox and debated popular teaching:** I found nothing on these sites for this chapter.
